d.title: Five numbers scaled down by three to four orders of magnitude
d.caption: The toy is not a simplification of the mechanism, only of the sizes — **one head where GPT-3 has 96, four dimensions where it has 12,288, six words where it has 50,257.** Every operation in the next three lessons is the real operation on these numbers. **Which is the point of working it by hand: there is nothing in a 175B model's forward pass that does not appear here**, so if the arithmetic below is followable, the architecture is understood.

d.title: Three words become three integers, and the text is never seen again
d.caption: **The stack receives integers and never sees the text again — so whatever the tokenizer decides is the model's entire view of the input.** One word per token here; a real tokenizer uses subwords, as 4.8 measured, **and nothing downstream cares.** Which is worth holding onto, because it means every tokenisation finding in module 4 is a finding about model capability rather than about preprocessing hygiene.

state: only this - the text is gone

d.title: Three vectors carrying identity and no order at all
d.caption: The lookup is the whole operation — **`E[0]`, `E[1]`, `E[2]`, three rows of a 6×4 table.** And the resulting matrix has a property worth naming before fixing it: **at this point the model cannot distinguish *“the cat sat”* from *“sat cat the”*, exactly as 4.9 proved for attention in general.** The vectors encode which words are present, in no particular arrangement.

d.title: One fast pair and one slow pair, which is the whole spectrum at d=4
d.caption: **At `d = 4` the four dimensions are `[sin(pos), cos(pos), sin(pos/100), cos(pos/100)]`** — the miniature version of 4.2's geometric spectrum. Read the columns: **the fast pair swings from 0.0000 to 0.9093 over three positions while the slow pair moves from 0.0000 to 0.0200.** So **the fast pair distinguishes adjacent positions and the slow pair would distinguish regions of a much longer sequence**, and the reference values reproduce exactly.

d.title: Position 0 turns [1,0,1,0] into all ones
d.caption: The addition is elementwise and the first row is instructive: **`E[the] + PE(0)` is `[1,0,1,0] + [0,1,0,1]` = `[1,1,1,1]`** — the positional encoding at position 0 is **not** a zero vector, so even the first token's representation is moved. And this `X` is now the only input the block will see: **three rows, four columns, with word identity and position already blended into the same four numbers and no way to separate them again.**

d.title: With Q = K = V = X the score matrix is symmetric, and 'sat' attends mostly to itself
d.caption: Setting all three projections to the identity makes the arithmetic minimal while every other step stays real — **and it exposes what the three matrices are for.** The score matrix is **symmetric**: `score(the,cat) = score(cat,the) = 4.3917`, because a dot product is symmetric and nothing distinguishes the two roles. And the result is degenerate: **`sat` gives 0.5101 of its attention to itself**, since a vector's largest dot product is usually with itself.

d.title: The toy matrices make the three roles visible: in order, swapped, and the other two dimensions
d.caption: **`W_Q` reads dimensions 0 and 1 in order, `W_K` reads the same two *swapped*, and `W_V` reads dimensions 2 and 3** — which is the minimal construction that makes the three vectors genuinely different. The analogy holds: **the query is what you type into a search box, the key is a page's indexed terms, and the value is the page content you actually read.** Note the consequence of the swap: **it breaks the symmetry §01 produced**, so `score(a,b) ≠ score(b,a)`.

d.title: Now 'sat' attends to 'cat' instead of to itself
d.caption: The same token now has three different vectors — **`q_sat ≠ k_sat ≠ v_sat`** — and `d_k` is **2, not 4**, because the head projects down. The scores change the outcome: **`score(sat→cat) = 3.4322` is now the highest, against `sat→sat` at 2.2297**, so the degenerate self-attention of §01 is gone. Scaling by `sqrt(2)` and softmaxing gives **[0.2651, 0.5149, 0.2200]**, matching the reference's [0.266, 0.516, 0.219].

d.title: The output is a weighted average of values, and dimension 1 comes out at exactly 1.0000
d.caption: **The weights multiply `v`, not `k`** — which is the step people skip, and it is why three matrices rather than two: **what is compared and what is handed over are different quantities.** The arithmetic is two lines, and dimension 1 lands on **exactly 1.0000** because all three values are ~1.0 there and the weights sum to 1. **So a dimension on which every token agrees passes through attention unchanged, however the weights fall.**

d.title: The residual restores the token, and the norm rescales what is left
d.caption: Adding `z_sat` back gives **[3.3341, 1.5044, 0.5226, 1.9997]** — and note dimension 0 is now 3.33, well outside the input's range, **which is 4.7's residual-stream growth happening in one step.** LayerNorm then brings it back: **μ = 1.8402, σ = 1.0132, and `n = [1.4745, -0.3315, -1.3005, 0.1574]` with mean 0 and variance 1.** Every figure matches the reference. **The norm is what keeps the next sublayer seeing inputs on a predictable scale.**

d.title: One dimension is zeroed, and that is the whole nonlinearity
d.caption: With identity weights and a 0.5 bias the FFN reduces to `ReLU(n + 0.5)`, **so the only thing it does is set −0.8005 to exactly 0.** That single clipped dimension is the entire nonlinearity in this block — **everything else in a transformer is a linear map or a normalisation**, which is worth sitting with: the FFN is where the model can express anything a matrix cannot. In a real model the same step runs **512 → 2048 → 512** with learned weights, clipping a different subset for every token.

d.title: The second residual and norm, and the block is done
d.caption: `r' = n + ffn_out` gives **[3.4490, −0.1629, −1.3005, 0.8148]**, and the variance has grown to **3.0791** — a wider spread than after the first norm, because the FFN's output was added to an already-normalised vector. The final hidden state is **`h = [1.5665, -0.4918, -1.1401, 0.0654]`**. And the scaling note: **in a 96-layer model these steps repeat 96 times, each writing another increment into this same vector** — here there is one layer, so the stack is done.

d.title: Six logits, each one dot product with an embedding row
d.caption: **With weight tying the projection matrix *is* the embedding matrix, so the logit for a word is `h` dotted with that word's embedding** — the same matrix that mapped ids to vectors on the way in. Which makes each logit readable: **`logit(mat) = h·[1,0,0,1] = 1.5665 + 0.0654 = +1.6319`**, two of `h`'s four numbers added. All six match the reference. **And look at the pairs: `the` at +0.4264 and `<eos>` at −0.4264** — which §06 explains.

d.title: “mat” at 47.51%, matching the reference to three decimals
d.caption: Six logits, one softmax, **probabilities summing to 1.000000 and every value matching the reference to three decimal places.** The prediction is `mat` at **47.51%** — which given a vocabulary containing both *on* and *mat* is **a defensible continuation of a sentence that wants to become *the cat sat on the mat*.** Note the distribution is not peaked: **the top two hold 0.747 between them**, so this toy model is uncertain in the way 5.8 measured GPT-2 being uncertain.

d.title: Every logit pair sums to exactly zero, and the cause is one line earlier
d.caption: **`logit(the) + logit(<eos>) = 0.000000` and so does every other pair** — which looks mysterious and is a direct consequence of two facts stacking. **LayerNorm makes `sum(h) = 0`, and this vocabulary's six embeddings are three complementary pairs** (`[1,0,1,0]` and `[0,1,0,1]` sum to all-ones). **So each pair's logits sum to `h · [1,1,1,1]` = `sum(h)` = 0.** An artefact of the toy vocabulary, and a clean demonstration that **a normalisation constraint propagates all the way to the output.**

d.title: Nine components, and the column most explanations skip is the middle one
d.caption: **The *why* is what most treatments leave out, and it is what makes the *how* memorable** — so each row below is the reason the component exists rather than its formula. Read them together and the architecture is a list of answers: **networks need numbers, ids have no similarity, attention cannot see order, a fixed state forgets, one head is one notion of relevance, parallel training must not leak the answer, attention only mixes, deep stacks need a gradient path, and dozens of layers need a stable scale.**

d.title: Seven matrices, and only one of them is not learned
d.caption: The origin column is the short answer to “where do the numbers come from”: **everything is learned except the positional encoding, which is a fixed formula — or learned too, depending on the variant** (4.9's first row). Worth reading the shapes together: **`W_Q`, `W_K` and `W_V` map `d_model` down to a head dimension, `W_O` maps back to `d_model`, and the FFN's pair expands and contracts** — so the only matrices that change the vector's width are the ones that put it back.

d.title: The same sentence, three weight choices, three different attention patterns
d.caption: This is the cleanest statement of what the weights do. **With identity projections `sat` attends to itself at 0.510. With real `W_Q` and `W_K` it attends to `cat` at 0.515. With the cheatsheet's weights it attends to `cat` at 0.661.** Same tokens, same positions, same mechanism — **the attention pattern is entirely a property of the learned matrices**, which is why 4.4's search for interpretable heads is a search through weights rather than through architecture.

d.title: W_K is a permutation of W_Q, so Q and K hold the same numbers reordered
d.caption: **Look at the `cat` rows: `Q` is `[1.851, 2.540, 1.841, 2.550]` and `K` is `[1.841, 2.550, 2.540, 1.851]` — the same four numbers in a different order.** That is the minimal way to make queries and keys genuinely different while keeping the arithmetic readable, and it is the same trick as 6.2's swap at larger `d`. **All six rows match the reference exactly**, which is what makes the rest of the trace trustworthy.

d.title: Raw scores near 16, scaled to 8, and the mask forcing row 0 to 1.000
d.caption: **The raw scores are all between 12 and 19 — large, because `d_k = 4` and the vectors are around 2.0 per component — and dividing by `sqrt(4) = 2` halves them**, which is 4.3's scaling doing its job on real numbers. Then the causal mask: **row 0 comes out `[1.000, 0.000, 0.000]`, which is forced rather than chosen** — the first token has one visible position, so its softmax is 1.0 whatever the score was. **Every value matches the reference.**

d.title: Four operations and the vector is back where it started, modified
d.caption: `Z = AV` gives **[0.987, 1.315, 0.908, 1.000]**, `W_O` maps it back to `d_model` as **[1.895, 2.223, 2.315, 1.987]**, and the residual add gives **[3.804, 2.807, 2.335, 2.987]**. Which makes 4.7's claim concrete: **the output of attention is roughly the same magnitude as the input, and the residual roughly doubles it** — so the block's contribution is comparable in size to what it was given, **and the normalisation that follows is not optional bookkeeping.**

d.title: Different weights, different logits, and the pairs still sum to zero
d.caption: **The logits are completely different from 6.3's — `cat` is now −1.8880 where it was −1.6319 — and every pair still sums to exactly 0.000000, with `sum(h) = 0.000000`.** Which confirms §06's explanation rather than restating it: **the antisymmetry does not depend on the weights at all. It follows from LayerNorm forcing the hidden state to sum to zero and the toy vocabulary's embeddings being complementary pairs** — a structural property, visible twice.

d.title: Two vocabularies, one architecture, and a target vocabulary that includes its own control tokens
d.caption: The source has three words and the target has five — **`<bos>` and `<eos>` are entries in the target vocabulary, not metadata**, which is what lets the decoder *predict* that it should stop. Everything else is minimal by design: **`d_model = 4`, one head, one encoder block, one decoder block.** The task is small enough to follow and structurally complete: **source reading, target writing, and the cross-attention between them.**

d.title: The same PE matrix is reused for source, target and every sentence
d.caption: The construction is identical to 6.1's — **and that is the point worth noticing: the positional encoding depends only on position and dimension, never on the token.** So **the same `PE` matrix serves the source and the target, and every sentence the model will ever see.** Which is why it costs zero parameters and why 4.9's extrapolation question is about a formula rather than about data: **nothing in `PE` was fitted to this sentence.**

d.title: Unmasked, so every row is a full distribution over all three source tokens
d.caption: **No triangle here — every source token attends to the whole sentence including positions after it**, which is the encoder's defining difference from 6.4's decoder and the reason 5.1 lists “cannot generate” against it. The weights are close to uniform on an untrained model (**0.176 to 0.553**), and the largest entry in every row is on `AI`, **which is an artefact of that token's embedding magnitude rather than anything semantic.**

d.title: One matrix, computed once, read at every decoding step
d.caption: Six operations — **self-attention, residual, LayerNorm, FFN, residual, LayerNorm** — produce a (3, 4) matrix. And its role is the thing to hold onto: **`memory` is computed once and reused at every decoder step** (6.7 counts one encoder pass against six decoder passes). Note all three rows have a strongly negative third dimension — **the encoder has pushed every source token in the same direction on that axis**, which is what a shared LayerNorm over four dimensions tends to produce.

d.title: Six steps, all shape-preserving, and only one of them mixes tokens
d.caption: Every row is **(3, 4) in and (3, 4) out** — the block never changes the shape, which is what lets blocks stack without adapters. And the “what it achieves” column separates the two kinds of work: **step 3 is the only one that mixes information between tokens**, while the embedding, positional add, FFN and both norms all operate on each row independently. **So an encoder block is one mixing operation surrounded by five per-token ones.**

d.title: The input is the target shifted right, which is how three predictions train in parallel
d.caption: **The decoder input is `[<bos>, ich, liebe]` and the target is `[ich, liebe, KI]` — the same sequence offset by one.** So position 0 is given `<bos>` and must predict `ich`, position 1 is given `<bos> ich` and must predict `liebe`, and position 2 is given both and must predict `KI`. **All three are scored in one forward pass, which is only legitimate because the causal mask stops position 0 seeing `ich` in its own input.**

d.title: Exactly zero above the diagonal, and row 0 is forced to 1.000
d.caption: **Upper-triangle maximum 0.00e+00**, as required — 4.5's `-inf` fill reproduced in a 3×3 matrix. And `<bos>`'s weight of 1.000 is **forced rather than chosen**, the same structural artefact 6.2 flagged: one visible position means a softmax of 1.0 whatever the score. The sublayer's job is narrow and worth naming: **it answers *“what have I written so far?”* and nothing else — it has no access to the English at all.**

d.title: Queries from the target, keys and values from the source — and no triangle
d.caption: **The shape is (3, 3) but it is target-by-source, not target-by-target — so there is nothing to mask: a German word may legitimately read any English word, including ones later in the sentence.** Rows sum to 1.0 over the **source**, which is 4.7's cross-attention measurement in miniature. This is the sublayer that answers *“what does the English say?”*, and it is the only place the two languages meet.

d.title: Maximum deviation from uniform: 0.0577
d.caption: This is what an untrained alignment looks like, quantified. **Uniform would be 0.333 in every cell and the largest deviation anywhere is 0.0577** — so the cross-attention matrix carries essentially no alignment information. The diagonal is **barely** favoured: **0.3500 mean on the diagonal against 0.3250 off it, a gap of 0.025.** Which is the honest reading of any attention map from an untrained model: **the structure people point to in trained alignment plots has to be learned, and here it is not there yet.**

d.title: The model predicts “liebe” at all three positions, and the loss is 2.532
d.caption: **Mean cross-entropy 2.532, matching the reference exactly** — and the per-position probabilities show why: **p(target) is 0.014, 0.436 and 0.081.** Position 1 scores well **by accident**, because the target there happens to be `liebe`. Which is the classic untrained signature: **mode collapse — one output token dominates regardless of input, at 0.762, 0.436 and 0.774** — and it is what the first few hundred training steps typically fix, **before the model learns anything about the task.**

d.title: Four steps, each one re-running the decoder over what it has built
d.caption: **Each step re-runs the decoder over the sequence so far, takes the distribution at the last position, picks a token and appends it** — and the loop ends when it picks `<eos>`, which is why §01 of 6.5 put that token in the vocabulary. **The encoder does not run again: `memory` was computed once and is reused at every step.** This is what the loop looks like **when the model works**; §02 is what this model actually did.

d.title: It emitted “liebe” five times and never stopped
d.caption: 6.6's mode collapse becomes a generation failure directly: **`liebe` at 0.762, then feeding it back gives `liebe` at 0.804, then 0.792, then 0.777, then 0.777** — and the probability **rises** at step 2 because the model now sees its own favourite token in its input. **It never picks `<eos>`, so there is no stopping condition and the loop runs to whatever length limit you set.** Which is the clearest demonstration of 4.5's exposure bias: **teacher forcing scored 0.436 at position 1, and free generation never gets there.**

d.title: One encoder pass and six decoder passes
d.caption: **The encoder runs once — `memory` is (3, 4) and computed one time — while the decoder runs once per generated token.** Which is the asymmetry that governs the cost of translation and of every encoder-decoder system: **source length is paid once and target length is paid per token.** It is also exactly where 5.2's KV cache applies: **the decoder's six passes re-attend over a prefix that grows each time, so caching the K and V of what is already written is the obvious saving.**

state: source paid once, target per token

d.title: Twelve steps, and the whole course so far fits in them
d.caption: Read it as the index it is. **Steps 1–2 are module 4's tokenisation and positional encoding, 3–6 are scaled dot-product attention, 7–8 are the residual, norm and FFN, 9–10 are the two masks, and 11–12 are the head and the loss.** Each line is one formula and one sentence, and every one of them has been computed by hand in this module. **The twelfth is the only one that is not part of the forward pass** — it is the number training pushes down.
